Can Simpler Boosting Beat a No-Model Forecast?

Out-of-sample evidence from the S&P 500, 2024–2025

ForecastingGradient BoostingMachine Learning

PublishedNovember 16, 2026AuthorScarlett Xie

Every trading day an investor makes a small bet on the next session: own the S&P 500, or step into cash. Nobody knows tomorrow’s winner; what a model can attempt is narrower and harder — which days to be out.

Can a simplified gradient-boosting model beat a no-model forecast of S&P 500 returns out of sample, and did its signals survive trading costs?

Saying “up” every day is already right 57.6% of the time, so a useful model has to beat that, not beat zero.

Data and a tradeable forecast

Daily S&P 500 closes from FRED, 2017–2025, a price index that excludes dividends.1 Each forecast uses nine numbers known at the close — the last five daily returns, cumulative return and volatility over 5 and 20 sessions — and targets one session’s return, in percentage points.

The model we started from

A gradient-boosted regression: 100 small trees added in sequence, each fitted to the error the previous ones left, the forecast being the historical average plus those corrections scaled by a learning rate (Figure 2); Table 1 lists the settings.

The original configuration leaves the model free to carve nine inputs into fine regions. On its training years it looks strong — a typical miss of 0.83 points against a target standard deviation of 1.22 — but out of sample its forecasts span only −4.0 to +2.2 points, are positive 74.5% of the time, and correlate with what happened at 0.05 (Figure 3).

It loses on every measure: root mean squared error 1.0550 against 1.0045, squared error 10.29% higher, direction accuracy 54.4% against 57.6%, and $100 becomes $127.82 rather than $146.56 (Tables 2 and 3).

Why daily returns are hard to forecast

The signal is tiny against the noise: the index moves about a point a session, any predictor explains a sliver, and misses are news rather than patterns. Relationships go stale as regimes change. And direction is a near-useless target, because “up” is already right 57.6% of the time. Flexibility only makes fitting noise cheaper.

What we changed

Three capacity cuts: learning rate 0.1 → 0.03, depth 3 → 1, minimum leaf 1 → 50 sessions. Each correction is trusted less, each tree may state a single condition, and a rule must hold for 50 sessions before it is used. A fourth change is procedural — the forecast window moves one session later, so the signal can be acted on (Figure 1).

Settings were chosen on 2022–2023 only: validation mean squared error falls from 1.66 to 1.48, 10.5% lower, and the three alternatives all scored worse.2

Table 1. The original and revised models side by side.

Original (classroom configuration) Revised
Trees 100 100
Questions per tree 3 (up to 8 leaves) 1
Learning rate 0.1 0.03
Minimum leaf 1 session 50 sessions
Forecast window session after the information date one session later, executable
Validation MSE, 2022–2023 1.66 1.48
Test RMSE, 2024–2025 1.0550 1.0063

How much better?

The benchmark repeats the pre-test average, 0.049% a day, and is hard to beat because it never chases noise; error is the root mean squared miss, which punishes large misses more.

The revision removes most of the handicap: squared error falls from 10.29% above the benchmark to 0.36%, and direction accuracy rises from 54.4% to 57.0%, though still not past the benchmark’s 57.6%. Yet the interval around the revised gap, −2.2 to +2.9%, contains zero, while the original’s, +2.4 to +19.8%, does not (Diebold–Mariano p = 0.055). It closes a gap without opening an advantage.

Table 2. Out-of-sample accuracy, 2024–2025 (502 sessions).

Forecaster RMSE (pp) Gap vs benchmark (%) 95% interval Direction accuracy (%)
Historical mean (benchmark) 1.0045 0.00 — 57.6
Five-session mean 1.1119 +22.53 +7.2 to +42.8 50.4
Original model 1.0550 +10.29 +2.4 to +19.8 54.4
Revised model 1.0063 +0.36 −2.2 to +2.9 57.0

Trading costs decide the verdict

Hold the index when the forecast is positive, zero-interest cash otherwise; orders at the next close; 5 basis points per one-way trade, including the first purchase and final sale.3

Staying invested turns $100 into $146.56; the original model $127.82, the revision $145.47 — 17.6 points recovered and 134 fewer trades. Before costs the revision leads, 48.70% against 46.70%, but 44 trades pay for that lead; what remains, 1.09 points (−14.6 to +15.9), is statistically nothing (Table 3).

Risk looks better — worst fall 13.58% against 18.90%, volatility 15.15% against 15.95%, Sharpe ratio 1.32 against 1.28 — but not generally: on 31 March 2025 its drawdown was 1.4 points deeper, and by December the two had converged. One week explains it: 7 of its 23 cash sessions fall in April 2025, including the index’s worst day; cash days averaged −0.048% against +0.088% invested.

Table 3. Two-year net return under three cost assumptions.

Strategy 0 bp 5 bp 10 bp
Hold the index throughout 46.70% 46.56% 46.41%
Original model 39.72% 27.82% 16.93%
Revised model 48.70% 45.47% 42.30%

Takeaway

The original model predicted badly — 10.29% worse squared error than a forecast needing no model, 178 trades, $127.82 per $100 — and cutting its freedom repaired that: 0.36%, 44 trades, $145.47. Repairing a handicap is not creating an edge, though: the interval contains zero, the return still trails buy-and-hold by 1.09 points, and the smaller drawdown rests on 23 cash sessions. Because the window was revised after earlier results were seen, these results stay exploratory.

Footnotes

  1. Data and trading sessions. S&P Dow Jones Indices LLC, S&P 500 via FRED. The price index excludes dividends. Missing closes and holidays are removed before returns are computed. Features use closing data through the information date; the target is the one-session return starting at the following close. FRED serves a rolling ten-year history, so the downloaded snapshot is retained with a checksum for exact replication.
  2. Model selection. Four revised configurations — learning rates of 0.01 to 0.1, depths of one to three, leaf minima of 10 to 50 — are compared on validation mean squared error, and the choice is fixed before the test years are touched. The original model follows the classroom materials: 100 trees, three questions per tree, learning rate 0.1, no minimum leaf size, nine predictors built from recent returns. The column labelled “original” re-estimates that configuration on this sample rather than copying a stored classroom output, so both models are trained on identical data and the comparison is like for like. Because the forecast window was revised after earlier results had been inspected, the revised test results remain exploratory.
  3. Investment assumptions. No leverage or short selling; cash earns zero. Five basis points means 0.05% per one-way trade, charged on portfolio value at the moment of the trade, including the initial purchase and the final sale. Dividends, cash interest, taxes and tracking error are omitted. The index is not directly tradable, so these are hypothetical index-exposure returns rather than observed ETF returns. Sharpe ratios annualize the mean daily return and divide by annualized daily volatility.

Reproducibility

The project sits beside the article: rendering index.qmd rebuilds every number, table and figure below. Place this folder at blog/posts/post9/ in the website project, open it in RStudio and press Render. The chunk at the top of the file runs code/analysis.py, which refits the models from data/raw/SP500.csv and rewrites result/; the article text then reads result/tables/numbers.csv, so no value is typed by hand. 

index.qmd                   article, layout and render entry point
README.md                   dependencies and replication steps
code/
├── analysis.py             runs the four stages below in order
├── run_model.py            data, features, splits, fitting, forecasts
├── evaluate_investment.py  trading rule, costs, DM tests, bootstrap intervals
├── make_figures.py         five 300-dpi figures
├── article_numbers.py      every value quoted in the text -> numbers.csv
└── test_pipeline.py        twelve checks on the saved outputs
data/
├── raw/SP500.csv           FRED download, unchanged, checksum verified
└── processed/              panel.csv, forecasts.csv
result/
├── figures/                five PNG figures
└── tables/                 metrics, inference, costs, numbers.csv, experiment.json

Required: R with knitr and rmarkdown, Quarto, and Python 3 with pandas, NumPy, scikit-learn, SciPy and Matplotlib. No internet connection is needed after setup. If R cannot find the right interpreter, set BLOG9_PYTHON to its full path. Every stage is seeded (20261116), writes only to data/processed/ and result/, and the four stages run in about five seconds, so a re-render reproduces the same tables and figures. The twelve tests in code/test_pipeline.py rebuild the target and lag features from the raw price file, recompute every metric from the saved forecasts, and check that costs only ever hurt and that the bootstrap is seed-deterministic.
